stories.title: MPs recommend BBC charter renewal is scrapped and licence fee is extended beyond TV
stories.summary: An parliamentary committee has published a new report as debate about the BBC's future continues.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 1 October 2026, 01:20 BST

The BBC licence fee should be extended to cover services other than TV and the corporation's charter review should be scrapped and made permanent, an influential group of MPs has said.

The report from the House of Commons' cross-party culture and media committee comes ahead of the government finalising its proposals for the next BBC royal charter later this year, which will set out how the broadcaster is funded, regulated and governed from 2028.

In its recommendations, the DCMS committee also said that political appointments to the BBC board should end, to improve public trust.

The report also said the next charter should be made permanent, so that the BBC's funding and existence is not called into question every 10 years.

They said the current renewal process "creates an avoidable opportunity for political interference which has damaged the perception of the BBC's independence".

"It also creates a disproportionate distraction for the BBC when it needs to be focused on its mission to inform, educate and entertain. We therefore recommend the next BBC charter be a permanent charter and not include an end date."

When making recommendations about the licence fee, the DCMS said its current model was "outdated and no longer fit for purpose", and also suggested that the BBC reduced the cost from its current price of £180 per year.

Schitt's Creek was snapped up by the BBC after the comedy series left Netflix

The committee also said the BBC should not pay "over the odds" for the rights to overseas hits such as Suits and Schitt's Creek.

Although the BBC produces a lot of its own programmes, the corporation buys some international shows for its TV channels and iPlayer streaming platform.

The MPs' report said the BBC could "spend more wisely when competing for programming".

Overall, the BBC brings "immeasurable benefits" to society but needs reform of the TV licence fee to avoid a fate of "managed decline", they said.

Committee chair Dame Caroline Dinenage said the report , external comes at "a pivotal moment for the BBC", which is grappling with changing media habits, declining income and negotiations with the government over how it is paid for.

Dame Caroline said the government "must ensure the BBC has a universal and sustainable source of funding".

But, she added, the BBC "can play its part by sweating its assets and boxing clever for the licence payer by ending illogical practices such as outbidding commercial rivals for overseas hits such as Suits, Schitt's Creek and Scooby Doo".

The rights to air all three programmes were bought by the BBC after contracts with other networks or streaming services expired.

"At a time of constrained resources, the BBC should not be paying over the odds for overseas content, particularly when it's a bidding war against commercial UK broadcasters," the committee said.

The MPs added that they "did not believe that this provides value for money for the licence fee payer".

The BBC argued that it spends less than 5% of its content budget on acquiring shows, less than other broadcasters, and they are a cost-effective way of delivering high-quality content to audiences who go on to discover homegrown programming.

Suits, starring the future Duchess of Sussex (second right, in 2012), has attracted new audiences in recent years

Dame Caroline said: "For all its faults, the BBC drives our creative economy, supports our democracy through media sovereignty, and delivers world-class entertainment and moments that bring us together.

"Like a much-loved family member, we may criticise and grumble about the BBC but we would miss it enormously if it were no longer here for us."

Licence fee 'not fit for purpose'

The committee said there were "considerable challenges" for the BBC and warned that the current TV licence fee is "outdated and no longer fit for purpose".

Currently, about 94% of individuals use the BBC each month but only 80% of households pay for a TV licence, the MPs noted.

"The licence fee should be reformed so it is no longer linked to the consumption of live TV or to a particular device, such as a television set," the committee said.

"This should be an easier sell to licence fee payers if expanding the base is paired with a drop in the individual cost."

The BBC's director-general Matt Brittin has previously described the current licence fee model as "a busted flush" and "yesterday's model", and has said the price could be cut if more people pay under an overhauled system.

The committee also suggested the BBC should:

Explore the opportunity for introducing an international TV licence so it can increase its revenue and global audience

Work with independent production companies who own the rights to many of its programmes to ensure more remain on iPlayer

Develop its current premises with facilities that can "harness the potential of new media and support the creator economy"

The committee suggested the government should:

Support the corporation by legislating to put a BBC button on remote controls for smart TVs

Press YouTube to give a certain level of prominence for content made by the BBC and other British public service broadcasters

Take back full funding for the BBC World Service, describing it as "the UK's number one soft power asset"

The committee supported opening up BBC iPlayer to shows from other public service broadcasters such as Channel 4.

Earlier this week, Channel 4 chief executive Priya Dogra said , external she was open to her network's content being hosted on iPlayer.

The report also called for the end of political appointments to the BBC board, to improve governance and remain trusted by the public.

And the committee recommended that the BBC is given new public purposes relating to innovation and technology and combating misinformation and disinformation.

The BBC welcomed the report, which it said made "some important and interesting recommendations on the future of the BBC".

A BBC spokesperson said: "We have consistently argued that the current funding model is outdated and needs reform, so we welcome the Committee's support for maintaining universal funding while overhauling the licence fee.

"We are also pleased to see their recognition of the vital work of the World Service, with a clear recommendation that responsibility for funding should return fully to Government.

"At a time of huge disruption in the media, the BBC's trust, reach and creative strength remain unparalleled. But we also recognise the need to evolve and move faster towards the future."

The government's Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) said it "agrees entirely with the Committee's conclusion that it is in the country's best interests for the next Charter to support an ambitious and innovative BBC, and that the corporation cannot be left to a future of managed decline".

A DCMS spokesperson added: "We will review and consider the committee's recommendations in detail, alongside the views of the public and other stakeholders, to inform decisions for the next Royal Charter."

Vape tax comes into effect - but prices won't rise yet
stories.summary: Vaping is about to becoming more expensive due to a new tax on products.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The government is trying to make vaping more expensive and less appealing to young people

Published 1 October 2026, 00:02 BST

The price of vapes is set to rise as a new tax comes into effect, with the aim of making vaping less attractive to children and young people.

The Vaping Product Duty will be imposed at a rate of £2.20 per 10ml of e-liquid. However, many customers will not see a jump in prices immediately, as sellers have six months to sell old stock at the pre-duty price.

The government wants to reduce the appeal of vapes by making them more expensive, as more evidence of its adverse effect on health comes out, particularly on children and young people.

The vaping industry has lobbied against the new tax, saying that affordable vapes help people to quit smoking.

The duty will apply to all vaping products regardless of whether they contain nicotine.

Tobacco rates were also raised on Thursday, by £2.20 per 100 cigarettes or 50g of tobacco. HMRC said this maintains the financial incentive for smokers to switch to vaping.

Stocking up v cutting down

The BBC spoke to vapers in Reading who had mixed views on whether the new tax would encourage people to quit.

Mackenzie Bird, 19, has been a regular vaper for three years. She said she was "fine" with the duty and it wouldn't stop her from vaping.

Mackenzie Bird said the tax wouldn't stop her from vaping

"I don't know how many people it'll actually deter," she said.

"I'll probably just stock up."

However, Cara Lewis-Rimes and Dylan Killner said they might reconsider the habit in light of higher prices.

Cara said she thinks the changes will force vapers to cut down because of the cost of living.

Cara and Dylan think the tax will prompt vapers to cut back

Dylan said he might be inclined to quit altogether.

"I don't think it's doing me any favours... the health factor around it as well is not great."

Fighting illegal trade

HMRC is also launching a stamp for vaping products which are traceable throughout the supply chain.

All vapes sold in the UK must carry this stamp from April.

The new tax is also an effort to combat illicit trade, which is a growing problem on UK high streets . Last month, the prime minister announced new powers for councils that will address the decline of the high street, including the amount of vape shops.

Changes to planning law in England mean every new shop selling e-cigarettes, or vapes, would need to apply to their local council for permission to open.

Health Minister Karin Smyth said: "These measures are an important step in our ambition to tackle youth vaping by reducing the affordability of vaping products, which goes hand-in-hand with the work we are already doing to tackle the appeal and availability of vapes on our high streets."

James Murray, the Financial Secretary to the Treasury, said the government was "backing all those retailers who play by the rules".

Vape shop staff like Jordan have seen customers stocking up ahead of the tax coming in

But Jordan Apap, a sales assistant in Berkshire Vapers, said the new tax would "put a lot of strain on legitimate vape shops" that provide more specialist advice and services than convenience stores and phone shops that sell vapes.

"There is a real and genuine risk that we will cease to exist within a year or two," he said.

Vaping rates for schoolchildren appear to drop - is it falling out of favour? Published 22 September

Police raid barbers and vape shops suspected of being fronts for crime gangs Published 10 April 2025

John Dunne, the director general of the UK Vaping Industry Association, said: "This is nothing short of a tax on public health."

He said vapes had helped "millions of adults cut down on or stop smoking".

"Protecting young people is essential. But that means stronger enforcement against illegal and rogue traders, not making legal vaping more expensive for adults trying to stay away from cigarettes."

Experts say vaping is much safer than smoking, but it is not risk free and the long-term effects are less clear.

A recent review of vaping studies found that it had an association with problems in children and young people including wheezing and coughing, poor oral and dental health, poor sleep, mental health problems and eye symptoms.

The NHS has said that children and non-smokers should never vape.

Fears that US deficit is unsustainable drive yields on Treasury bills and UK gilts to multi-decade highs

Business live – latest updates

The turmoil in global bond markets has intensified amid fears the US deficit is reaching unsustainable levels, helping drive UK long-term borrowing costs to a 28-year high.

The threat of a renewed round of inflation from the persistently high cost of oil has spooked investors, who believe central banks will be forced to raise interest rates in the coming months to prevent price increases from becoming embedded.

In a morning of hectic trading on Thursday, the yield, which is a proxy for the interest rate, hit 6% on Britain’s 30-year bonds for the first time since 1998.

The yield on five- and 10-year UK bonds also rose, driving up the government’s borrowing costs and adding to the pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before the budget later this month.

The sell-off also drove US government borrowing costs to 24-year highs on Thursday, with 10-year Treasury bill yields hitting 5.34%.

Thirty-year US Treasury bond yields rose above 5.67%, hitting their highest level since May 2002.

Stock market investors also sold heavily, knocking 1.7% off the FTSE 100 in London during early trading. Bourses in other parts of Europe were also hit, with Germany’s Dax and France’s CAC 40 falling by 1.1%.

“There is carnage in the bond market which is hitting stocks hard,” said Neil Wilson, the investor strategist at Saxo UK. “It looks like the relentless rout in the bond market is sending investors running for cover.”

By midday in the UK, the sell-off had eased, pulling the 30-year bond yield back below 6% and lifting share prices off their lows.

But yields then pushed higher in afternoon trading, back over the 6% mark.

The bond sell-off around the world is being driven by fears of high inflation, as the Middle East conflict continues to restrict oil supplies from the region.

Japan’s 10-year yield rose towards the 30-year high set last month.

after newsletter promotion

US bonds weakened despite inflation data on Wednesday coming in lower than forecast, which was expected to calm investors’ nerves about the prospect of further increases in the cost of borrowing by the US Federal Reserve.

Traders remain anxious that the Fed will continue to raise interest rates to fight inflation, mainly in response to the strength of the US economy and the prospect of workers bidding up their wages.

Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies, said there was growing concern at the amount of debt being issued to fund government deficits, as well as inflation concerns.

“Inflation, deficit and issuance concerns continue to weigh on the bond market,” he said.

“There is also a buyers’ strike as investors do not want to step in till we get some form of stability. Hedge funds have suffered in the latest round of sell-off and do not have the risk appetite to fade the move. Real money, potentially has the risk appetite, but won’t step in till we get some stability.”

Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “While the latest data has reduced expectations of an October Fed rate hike, investors remain wary that persistent inflation and higher oil prices could keep rates elevated for longer.

“The dollar is benefiting from that caution, climbing to a three-month high, while the prospect of a December rate increase keeps pressure on bond markets.”

stories.title: Could changing the pension triple lock pay for Burnham's big social care plan?
stories.summary: Burnham said he wants to change the pensions triple lock from 2030 to pay for his social care reform, but analysts have questioned whether it will raise enough money.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 29 September 2026

In his Labour conference speech, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would "adjust" the triple lock on the state pension to help pay for a new "national care service" in England from 2030.

While his proposed reform is likely to reduce public spending on pensions, analysts say it would be unlikely to save enough money between 2030 and 2040 to pay for comprehensive social care reform.

BBC Verify has looked at the key figures.

What is the planned triple lock reform?

Since it was introduced by the coalition government in 2011, the triple lock has guaranteed that the UK state pension rises each year in line with whichever is the highest of inflation, average wages, or 2.5%.

Burnham said that from April 2030, instead, it would only rise in line with the highest of inflation or 2.5%.

The prime minister added that "it will hold its value relative to earnings over time".

We are still awaiting full details from the government, but the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) think tank , external says the new proposed system would ensure that the state pension rises by whichever is highest of:

inflation

2.5%

average earnings over time rather than every year

The IFS says the key change is that the state pension will not automatically jump up with average wage increases every year, but only broadly track them over a longer period of time.

That is important because in some years the triple lock has meant the state pension has risen faster than earnings.

"The removal of this permanent ratchet is to be welcomed and marks a substantial step towards a more sustainable and predictable state pension system," the IFS says.

It estimates that the present triple lock will increase annual state pension expenditure by £16bn a year by 2026–27, compared with if it had risen in line with average earnings growth since 2011.

It says that if the new lock had been in place instead, spending would be £9bn a year lower than it currently is.

There is considerable uncertainty about future savings though because the cost of the triple lock is linked to the future volatility of people's earnings and inflation, which are impossible to confidently forecast.

Burnham vows to end existing pension triple lock in 2030 to help fund care Published 1 day ago

Faisal Islam: Triple lock move is significant, but it's a gamble Published 1 day ago

Andy Burnham wants to fix social care - what are the options? Published 3 days ago

What is the triple lock and why are people talking about it? Published 1 day ago

Moreover, analysts think it could take more than a decade for the reform to deliver major savings.

Earlier this year, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) - the government's official forecaster - analysed how much , external shifting to just an earnings-linked state pension in 2030 would cost relative to keeping the triple lock.

This is similar to what Burnham is proposing.

The OBR did not identify any significant savings for the government from such a shift until 2034.

By 2040, the annual saving was estimated by the OBR to be 0.2% of GDP, equivalent to £6bn a year in today's money.

Downing Street has said the prime minister's planned change will save £15bn a year by the end of the 2030s , external , equivalent to £11bn a year in today's money, but it did not provide detail on how it reached this figure.

The IFS estimates that the reform will save around £4bn a year, in today's money, by 2035.

But it cautions that future savings are "very uncertain" and says the change "could easily save nothing at all if earnings growth is strong".

How much would social care reform cost?

Different social care reforms come with different price tags.

The Health Foundation think tank has estimated that imposing a lifetime cap on an individual's care costs of around £86,000 in England, as proposed by the official report for the coalition government by Andrew Dilnot in 2011, would cost the government around £4bn a year.

The think tank estimates that introducing a Scotland-style system of "free personal care" - which does not include accommodation, food and everyday living costs - would amount to around £7.5bn a year.

And the cost of creating a universal and comprehensive social care system , external in England would be around £18.5bn a year extra by 2036.

The government has not set out the full details of how the "national care system" will work, but has clarified that while an individual's direct care costs would be covered, their accommodation costs in a residential or nursing home would not be.

Nevertheless, if it implemented a universal and comprehensive social care system then the expected revenues from the proposed reform could fall short.

Jonathan Cribb of the IFS said the pension reform "will not be the answer to funding universal social care".

This could put pressure on a future government to raise revenues from other sources - either from tax rises or spending cuts elsewhere - to pay for a comprehensive social care service in England.

This article was updated on 30 September to include new IFS analysis of future savings from the change to the state pension lock.

stories.title: Grooming gangs inquiry expanded to Birmingham and Wales
stories.summary: Targeted investigations will be carried out as part of a national inquiry into child sexual abuse.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The national inquiry involves a series of targeted, local investigations into child sexual abuse by grooming gangs

Published 30 September 2026

A national inquiry into child sexual abuse by grooming gangs has announced that targeted investigations will take place in Birmingham and Wales.

The inquiry said the probes would "examine the sexual abuse and exploitation of children by grooming gangs and the response of organisations responsible for protecting children" in both areas.

Oldham in Greater Manchester, Bradford and Keighley in West Yorkshire and London were announced as the first locations for investigations earlier this year.

It is unclear whether further locations will be selected. Some survivors have expressed frustration that their area has not yet been included and said they were concerned about expanding the inquiry's scope.

Fiona Goddard, who was sexually abused as a child by groups of men in Bradford, said there was clearly evidence from Birmingham and Wales "that needs to be properly heard" and welcomed their inclusion.

But she told the BBC that the scale of the inquiry "must not come at the expense of the depth of investigation". This was especially concerning, Goddard added, given "we are already almost a year into the inquiry with relatively little progress".

Carly, not her real name, was 12 years old when she was first groomed in Huddersfield in 2004. She said she could not understand "how an investigation covering an area as enormous and complex as Wales can be described as a deep dive".

"How are survivors in Huddersfield supposed to have confidence that our experiences will not simply be absorbed into a much bigger national picture and effectively watered down?"

Meanwhile, Welsh grooming gang victim Emily Vaughan, not her real name, welcomed the announcement - saying it marked "a day that has been needed for a very long time".

"It's about institutions that failed children and the questions that have remained unanswered. The expansion of the inquiry means those failures can no longer simply be brushed aside."

Fiona Goddard, pictured last year, said Wednesday's announcement left "important questions unanswered"

The Statutory Independent Inquiry into Grooming Gangs in England and Wales was announced by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer in June 2025 and started work in April.

It previously faced turbulence prior to launching, when abuse survivors called on former safeguarding minister Jess Phillips to quit amid claims that the government was seeking to widen the scope of the inquiry to other forms of child abuse.

Chaired by former children's commissioner Baroness Anne Longfield, it has the power to compel individuals and institutions to explain what they "did or did not do to protect children from being sexually abused".

Alongside national accountability hearings, local investigations will examine what happened in specific areas, including how grooming gangs operated and what institutions knew.

The inquiry has previously said that areas are chosen for investigation based on criteria including how victims and survivors were treated when they came forward, and whether opportunities to prevent harm were missed.

A National Listening Project, inviting victims and survivors to share their experiences, has also been expanded, with people able to contribute through written or recorded submissions from next month.

But Amy Clowrey, a director at Switalskis solicitors, which represents more than 50 survivors who are participating in the national inquiry, warned that clarity was needed over how evidence "from places without a local investigation" would be examined by the inquiry.

First locations for grooming gang inquiry announced Published 24 June

Hundreds of my abusers are still out there, says victim as grooming inquiry launched Published 31 March

Vital paperwork for grooming gangs inquiry may be lost, say MPs Published 27 March

The inquiry said its decision to conduct an investigation in Birmingham reflected a combination of factors "including victim and survivor experience, indications of prevalence, harm and risk, and public concern".

Panel member Zoë Billingham said: "We will look carefully at what organisations knew, how decisions were made, how agencies worked together, and why opportunities to protect children were missed".

The Birmingham investigation may extend to surrounding or connected areas if the evidence supports it.

Phillips, Labour MP for Birmingham Yardley, welcomed the move. She praised Baroness Longfield as an "amazing and robust" public servant, adding that those already taking part in the inquiry "felt that they've been heard".

But she said her main hope for the inquiry was for it to create "the impetus for change", adding that she did not want the process "to go on for decades".

Birmingham Local Conservatives, which had previously called for the city's grooming cases to be fully investigated, also welcomed the announcement - saying questions had gone unanswered for too long.

The investigation in Wales will also examine the operation of devolved arrangements and cross-border working between organisations in Wales and England.

The Welsh government welcomed the announcement, and said minister Delyth Jewell had met Baroness Longfield earlier this week to press for "dedicated activity" in Wales as part of the national inquiry.

The Welsh Conservatives and Reform also supported the news. Both parties have previously called for a Wales-only grooming gangs inquiry, but failed to win support from the government under both Welsh Labour and Plaid Cymru.

stories.title: Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham
stories.summary: The PM says a referendum wouldn't be the right thing now but the UK needs to consider its options for the future.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 30 September 2026

Andy Burnham has said it is "possible" a future Labour election manifesto could promise a new in-out referendum on the European Union.

The prime minister told the BBC a referendum "wouldn't be the right thing to do right now" but the UK needed to "consider the options" for its relationship with the EU as "where we are isn't good enough".

It comes after he pledged in his Labour conference speech on Tuesday to explore closer ties with the bloc at a summit later this year.

The move could set up a huge dividing line at the next general election, with the Conservatives accusing Burnham of trying to "reopen old wounds by restarting the battles of the Brexit years".

As a candidate in the Makerfield by-election that propelled his return to Parliament, Burnham had promised not to "re-run" Brexit arguments and said he was "not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU".

In an interview with BBC political editor Chris Mason, Burnham was challenged over whether he was reopening divisive arguments about rejoining the EU, despite promising not to in May.

In response, the PM said: "No, I'm not proposing that, am I? I am saying that in a context when we're looking at a 10-year plan for Britain, Britain needs to consider the options as to where we will be.

"That is way before you even get to anything that's put before the public, this is about now just looking at what are the broad options for our relationship."

He suggested these options could include staying "exactly as we are", a closer relationship similar to that being discussed by the EU and Canada or rejoining the EU customs union.

However, Burnham stressed that "to leap back to a proposal and a referendum on it wouldn't be the right thing to do right now".

Pressed over whether including an in-out referendum in a future Labour manifesto was a possibility, Burnham said: "Yes, things are possible. I think where we are isn't good enough."

Chris Mason: Burnham delivers deeply political speech with a personal core Published 1 day ago

Five takeaways from Andy Burnham's Labour conference speech Published 1 day ago

Davey promises tax cuts for millions if UK rejoins EU single market Published 22 September

Asked earlier on BBC Radio 4's Today if he wanted the UK to rejoin the EU, Burnham replied that he wanted to "look at the options".

The PM added that he had previously advocated such a move within his lifetime, whilst acknowledging it was "not necessarily the case that that is now".

French President Emmanuel Macron said it would be "very good news" if the UK wanted to rejoin the EU, while Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said his country would welcome Britain back "with open arms".

Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey said his party had put forward "concrete plans to boost our economy, strengthen our defences and cut people's taxes by joining the single market and a customs union".

He added: "Talk is cheap. Burnham must stop with all the 'maybes' and get negotiating that better deal for Britain today."

The party's Europe spokesperson Al Pinkerton said last week there is "no rejoin on the table", adding Britain would effectively be treated as a "fresh entrant state" if it wished to join the bloc again.

Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice accused Burnham of "trying to sneak us back into Brussels via the back door".

Tice said: "He says Brexit has done more harm than good but what's done real harm is a Labour government that can't deliver growth, can't control migration and now wants to outsource the job to Brussels."

He added Reform would "never let this betrayal go unchallenged".

In his Labour conference speech on Tuesday, Burnham blamed Brexit for a loss of control over both immigration and the economy, telling delegates he did not believe the current relationship was "good enough".

He told activists he wanted to use the rescheduled summit later this year to lay out "different options" for the UK's long-term relationship with Europe.

He promised to "find consensus" on an option to clarify the UK's position, although did not offer further detail of how this would be measured.

In response to Burnham's conference speech, Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart said: "Labour cannot pin the blame for their disastrous economic decisions on a vote that happened over a decade ago.

"Besides, they are already dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset."

Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "All Andy Burnham offers on repairing our relationship with our biggest trading partner is a promise to keep our options open.

"The Green Party is very clear that we should rejoin the customs union to start reversing the damage, and full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK."

stories.title: Household energy bills forecast to see biggest rise in four years
stories.summary: A typical household faces an annual gas and electricity bill of £1,999 from January, based on a key forecast.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 30 September 2026

Household energy prices are set to soar in January, with a typical annual bill forecast to jump by £276, figures shared with the BBC reveal.

The 16% predicted increase would hit millions of households at the coldest time of year, and would mark the biggest rise in bills for four years.

The forecast from consultancy Cornwall Insight comes a day before prices go up under regulator Ofgem's October price cap and puts increased pressure on the government to support those who will struggle to pay.

Meanwhile, the boss of supplier EDF Simone Rossi has warned the UK is "walking into a second energy crisis" and called for an extension to the VAT cut on electricity which kicks in on Thursday.

Energy prices bite in winter

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told BBC Radio 4's Today programme he would not call Rossi's crisis warning an overstatement, adding that the cost of home energy, as well as petrol and diesel, was "very difficult indeed".

Speaking from the Labour conference in Liverpool, he added: "We're looking at any measure that can give people breathing space, that can take the pressure off."

About 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales are on variable energy tariffs set by Ofgem's price cap, which puts a maximum price on each unit of gas and electricity.

Those homes will see a 4% increase in prices on Thursday, the equivalent of about £60 per year – or £5 per month – taking an annual bill to £1,723 for the typical household using both electricity and gas and paying by direct debit if this level was sustained for a year.

That rise would have been higher without the government's VAT cut, which knocks the equivalent of about £45 a year off a typical bill.

But forecasts show a far greater increase is possible for bills in January. Cornwall Insight said its latest forecast suggests the typical annual bill would rise to £1,999.

The forecast 16% rise will come at the worst time of year, according to Craig Lowrey, principal consultant at Cornwall Insight.

"These prices are going to hit households hard. January is already a difficult month for many, with cold weather and bank balances still recovering from Christmas," he said.

The predicted rise is the result of disruption of gas supplies owing to the conflict in the Middle East, and the resulting low gas storage levels in Europe. Rebuilding those stocks could mean high bills "well beyond the winter", the forecaster said.

Cornwall Insight has a strong track record on forecasts and is widely respected across the industry and politics. Similar forecasts have been made by energy suppliers.

What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills? Published 3 days ago

Four ways to keep your energy bills down Published 8 hours ago

This remains only a prediction at this stage. Ofgem will not announce the actual January price change until late November.

While an easing of tensions in the Middle East could lessen the pain for billpayers, the price setting period for the January cap is already halfway through.

With little sign of a truce or lower international energy costs, a big increase in prices for those not on a fixed tariff looks highly likely. Lowrey said a January rise was "all but certain".

'Everything's going up'

Aaron Richards says it feels like all his costs are going up

That will be tough for people like Aaron Richards from Maidenhead.

"I try to eat less takeaways, work more overtime, and try to budget a bit better, but at the same time, we shouldn't have to," he said.

Aaron drives a diesel car, and so is paying record high prices to travel to and from work.

"I just feel like everything's going up. How far is it going to go? Someone's got to step in," he said.

"I know people who can't afford to heat their house and they're struggling at the moment. Housing and eating are two of life's essentials that everyone should have. It shouldn't be a challenge to have any of those things."

Years of relatively high domestic energy bills have left some people facing big sums in unpaid bills.

Recent data from Ofgem showed that customers collectively owe more than £5bn in unpaid bills and charges to suppliers.

The regulator has a proposed debt relief scheme on the table, and campaigners keep telling them to get on with it, urging the government to provide funding for it to be implemented.

"This is unsustainable, not just for households but also for the market as a whole," said Adam Scorer, chief executive of fuel poverty charity National Energy Action.

"The Budget must deliver additional targeted support for households most at risk this winter, alongside action to tackle energy debt and improve the least energy-efficient homes."

Among others calling for government help for struggling billpayers is Simone Rossi, chief executive of supplier EDF Energy.

Speaking exclusively to the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast, Mr Rossi said: "We are actually walking into a second significant energy crisis after the one we experienced just four years ago."

He said that the government should extend the cut in VAT on electricity bills from 5% to 0% beyond April, when it is due to expire.

He also urged ministers to give the go-ahead to the new Jackdaw gas field off the coast of Aberdeen, and the Rosebank oil field off Shetland.

stories.title: While the Country Rejects ALPR Mass Surveillance, SF Settles for Weak Safeguards
stories.summary: San Francisco's decision to retain its use of Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) surveillance cameras belies what we know about this spying technology tool: it endangers residents and threatens the privacy and civil liberties of our community. Based on what's in the city's press release and announcement, this policy will do nothing to stop actual harms. We know innocent drivers will be stopped and menaced by officers because of erroneous matches . We know officers use Flock to stalk potential and past romantic partners . Data will be accessed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and used to deport immigrants . Promising greater penalties for such abuse will not end this. These are not isolated mistakes that another policy can fix. They are consequences of building a system that records everyone’s movements and makes them searchable by police. This is also not unique to a single vendor. From Flock Safety to Motorola to Axon—San Francisco must end its use of ALPRs. We ultimately cannot rely on new protocols from city officials, and the City’s new policy is woefully inadequate. There is no warrant requirement to search stored ALPR data. An incident or computer-aided dispatch (CAD) number is not judicial authorization. Without a warrant requirement, officers can search stored location data without showing probable cause to a judge, and will. Without judicial control, officers will continue to search the data for abusive reasons. But a warrant requirement alone would not justify retaining the ALPR network: the community is demanding an end to the collection itself. Additionally, the announced policies include no deadline to delete ALPR data, there is only a 30-day deadline to move data from the vendor’s servers to the city’s servers. City officials must understand that moving data is not deleting it. Whether Flock or SFPD stores the data, it remains a permanent record of where people drive, worship, work, organize, seek care, and spend time with others. Thus, the best practice is deletion. New Hampshire requires deletion in three minutes, and Flock itself has reduced the default retention time to seven days. San Francisco can and should do better. stories.title: Privacy’s Defenders Podcast: Cowboys, Cypherpunks and Visionaries
stories.summary: People are increasingly concerned about the ways in which mass surveillance is tracking our every move: from Flock license plate readers to face recognition to creepy ads that – based on what we see and do online – seem to know everything we’re thinking and planning. It didn’t have to be this way, and since the early days of the internet, a dedicated band of activists, lawyers and technologists have fought for a better, more secure and private digital future – a future that’s still attainable. Cindy Cohn, who just finished a 26-year run with the Electronic Frontier Foundation including 11 years as its executive director, has lived this fight. She says privacy isn’t just about secrecy: It's ultimately about power – who has it, and who has the ability to protect themselves from it. It’s a story of the Secret Service’s “Operation Sundevil,” jet-setting tech titans, tie-dyed cypherpunks, and a fateful house party in San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury district amid the earliest days of online communications, setting the stage for the battles that created the internet as we know it and issues we still grapple with today.
